title: Feed farm animals in accordance with a planned diet

lessons.title: Feeds and the planned diet
lessons.html:
Feeds and the planned diet

Animals need the right food in the right amount to grow, stay healthy and produce milk, meat, eggs or wool. The farm manager or a feed adviser makes a planned diet (ration) for each group of animals. Your job is to feed exactly according to that plan.

What is in feed

  • Energy: from grain such as maize, and from molasses. Gives power for work, growth and milk.
  • Protein: from oilcake (soya, sunflower, cotton), lucerne and other legumes. Builds muscle and milk.
  • Fibre (roughage): from grass, hay, silage and straw. Cattle, sheep and goats (ruminants) need fibre for their rumen to work.
  • Minerals and vitamins: from licks and premixes. Salt, phosphate and others keep bones and the body healthy.
  • Water: the most important nutrient of all. Animals must always have clean water.

Different animals, different diets

Animal groupTypical feeding
Beef cattle on veldGrazing plus a lick in winter
Dairy cowsGood roughage plus concentrate measured to milk production
Feedlot cattle and lambsMixed ration with grain, roughage and additives
PigsMeal or pellets for each stage: piglet, grower, finisher, sow
Broilers and layersStarter, grower, finisher or layer mash, bought ready-mixed

Reading the feeding plan

The plan tells you which feed, how much, how often and for which pen or camp. For example: "Pen 4 weaners: 2 kg creep pellets per head per day, split morning and afternoon." If something on the plan is unclear, ask before you feed.

Changing feed slowly

Ruminants must get used to a new feed over several days. A sudden change to a lot of grain can cause acidosis or bloat, which can kill animals. Follow the change-over plan.

lessons.title: Preparing, measuring and giving feed
lessons.html:
Preparing, measuring and giving feed

Measuring

  • Weigh feed on a scale, or use a scoop or bucket that has been measured (calibrated) so you know how many kilograms it holds.
  • Work out the total: number of animals x amount per animal. For example, 30 ewes x 0.5 kg = 15 kg.
  • Do not guess. Too little feed and animals lose condition; too much wastes money and can make them sick.

Checking the feed

Before feeding, look at and smell the feed. Do not feed:

  • mouldy, wet, hot or caked feed;
  • feed with a bad smell or with rat droppings;
  • feed that is meant for another type of animal. Some feeds, such as those with urea or certain additives, can poison other animals. For example, feed with urea is made for ruminants and must never be given to horses or pigs.

Feeding

  1. Feed at the same times every day. Animals like routine.
  2. Spread feed along the trough so all animals can eat and the weak ones are not pushed out.
  3. Check there is enough trough space for the number of animals.
  4. Make sure clean water is available. Clean the water troughs.
  5. Watch the animals eat. Note animals that do not come to eat; they may be sick.
  6. Check how much is left at the next feed. Leftovers or empty troughs tell the manager whether the amount is right.

Storing feed

  • Store bags on pallets, off the floor and away from walls, in a dry, closed store.
  • Keep rats, birds and animals out of the store.
  • Use the oldest feed first and check expiry dates.
  • Keep feed away from fertiliser, fuel and chemicals.

Records

Record the date, pen, feed type and amount fed, and any leftovers or problems.

Safety

Lift bags with bent knees, use a dust mask in dusty feed rooms, and keep hands out of mixers and augers.

Key points

  • Feed exactly according to the planned diet for each group.
  • Feeds supply energy, protein, fibre, minerals and vitamins; water is always needed.
  • Weigh or measure feed; never guess.
  • Never feed mouldy feed or feed meant for another animal type; change feeds slowly.
  • Watch the animals, check leftovers and record everything.
